responses.strategic_rationale: This early-stage clinical research facility must navigate three fundamental tensions: (1) capturing rare parasomnia events requires prolonged residential observation, but extended stays risk participant dropout and inflate operational costs; (2) naturalistic behavior monitoring demands a domestic environment, yet safety and regulatory compliance push toward clinical infrastructure; (3) high-quality event annotation requires skilled manual scoring, but manual review capacity is finite and introduces rater variability. The levers below address recruitment sustainability and event yield, physical facility design and operational scalability, data quality and annotation workflow, and the algorithmic support system — balancing scientific rigor against cost control and staff burnout.

levers.name: Stay Duration and Event-Yield Trade-Off
levers.consequences: Longer residential stays increase the probability of capturing rare parasomnia events (critical for Aim 2 phenotyping), but extend participant burden, reduce recruitment appeal, and amplify operational costs per completed participant. Conversely, shorter fixed stays lower costs and improve recruitment, but risk low event capture and high unproductive admissions — potentially triggering the 20% ceiling early and forcing painful recruitment-criteria revision.
options: Fix stay duration at 14 days for all participants regardless of captured events, prioritizing operational predictability and cost control even if 25–30% of admissions yield no adjudicated events.

Implement a three-tier stay framework — baseline 10 days for all participants, plus 7-day optional extension for those with subthreshold event activity, plus a final 14-day extension slot reserved for promising high-yield participants identified by mid-stay technician assessment.

Adopt a rolling admission model with variable 2–4 week stays calibrated individually by pre-admission sleep history (frequency, injury severity, bed-partner corroboration strength), accepting recruitment complexity but maximizing event yield per participant-night.
levers.review_lever: Longer stays increase event capture but spiral operational costs and threaten recruitment feasibility; shorter stays improve throughput but risk enrolling many non-productive participants, violating the 20% unproductive ceiling and forcing expensive protocol amendments mid-study.

levers.name: Facility Expansion and Staffing Scalability
levers.consequences: The 8-suite launch is operationally safe with 3 technicians rotating nights, but moving to the deferred 12-suite expansion requires recruiting and training additional staff, proportionally increasing the payroll footprint. Understaffing expansion (e.g., 3 technicians covering 12 suites) risks delayed event response, incomplete annotations, and staff burnout, whereas overstaffing before event-yield and data quality mature wastes budget and creates idle capacity.
options: Freeze at 8 suites through the 3-year period, accepting a maximum enrollment cap of 65–70 participants but preserving tight staffing margins and deferring expansion risk entirely to a Phase 2 proposal.

Pilot 10 suites in year two (hiring 1 additional technician after month 18 go-live data review) if year-one event capture and annotation throughput metrics justify the incremental cost, with final decision gated by month 15 SAB review.

Provision all 12 suites in year two with a full staffing complement (4 technicians), aggressively pursuing higher enrollment targets (40–50 participants per year) to offset fixed facility costs, contingent on securing supplemental pharma funding to bridge the higher payroll commitment.
levers.review_lever: Premature expansion to 12 suites stretches thin staffing and inflates payroll without proven event yields or annotation capacity; deferring expansion preserves financial safety but caps enrollment and may leave the 36-month publication target vulnerable if year-one participant yield underperforms.

levers.name: Domestic Ambiance Versus Clinical Safety and Audit Trail
levers.consequences: A converted residential property with padded corridor edges and muted institutional signage fosters naturalistic sleep behavior, but introduces ambiguity in facility design documentation, complicates regulatory inspection, and creates grey zones in incident reporting when injury occurs in a non-obviously "clinical" space. Conversely, retrofitting the property with explicit clinical signage, visible safety equipment, and sterile aesthetic accelerates regulatory approval and audit trail clarity but may suppress the parasomnia phenotype through environmental cue-induced suppression.
options: Maintain intentionally residential aesthetics (soft lighting, domestic furnishings, minimal visible clinical apparatus) with a parallel detailed design-rationale document for regulatory bodies explaining that suppression of parasomnia behavior due to overt clinical environment directly threatens study validity and scientific aims.

Adopt a dual-identity approach: public-facing spaces (lounge, dining, corridors) are residential and naturalistic; private sleep suites contain visibly mounted safety rails, emergency call systems, and prominent facility signage, compartmentalizing clinical identity to the sleep environment itself.

Convert the property to explicit clinical décor and signage from the outset, accepting potential behavioral suppression as a necessary trade-off for regulatory streamlining, faster inspection approvals, and unambiguous incident documentation, with baseline comparison across the matched control cohort to quantify any phenotype dampening.
levers.review_lever: Residential aesthetics enhance naturalism but blur clinical identity and invite regulatory scrutiny; clinical décor simplifies compliance but may suppress the rare parasomnia events the study exists to capture, requiring explicit controls to measure artifact.

levers.name: Tiered Sensor Acquisition and Data Burden
levers.consequences: Continuous low-burden monitoring (dry EEG, mattress sensors, infrared, ambient microphones) runs every night for all participants, capturing rare events at low cost but generates massive raw data volumes and false-positive noise. Scheduled enhanced-night PSG (first, mid-stay, final) provides clinical-grade resolution for validation but covers only 3 of ~30 nights and misses sporadic events outside those windows. Escalation nights add targeted clinical-grade capture after technician flags but require real-time judgment calls and rapid setup, introducing operational latency and technician fatigue.
options: Deploy continuous low-burden monitoring nightly for all participants, with no scheduled enhanced nights; conduct enhanced PSG only reactively after a technician-flagged event, accepting gaps in clinical-grade data outside those windows but maximizing cost efficiency and sensor uptime simplicity.

Mandate enhanced PSG nightly for all participants from start of stay, guaranteeing clinical-grade data completeness but incurring higher equipment costs, participant discomfort, and technician setup burden that may compromise enrollment appeal and staff retention.

Execute continuous low-burden monitoring on all nights plus scheduled enhanced PSG on nights 1, 7, 14, and 21 (if stay is extended), providing clinical-grade snapshots at week cadence while reducing nightly enhanced-PSG burden compared to daily application.
levers.review_lever: Continuous low-burden monitoring maximizes data volume but floods the annotation pipeline with noise; daily enhanced PSG guarantees clinical resolution but inflates equipment costs and participant burden; scheduled enhanced nights balance coverage against cost but risk missing sporadic events outside the sampling windows.

levers.name: Event-Triage Algorithmic Support and Manual Annotation Workflow
levers.consequences: Semi-automated event-triage tools (Aim 3 deliverable) are intended to rank probable parasomnia episodes and reduce manual review burden, but developing and validating these tools requires extensive labeled training data, iterative refinement, and extensive dual-human scoring for ground-truth comparison — creating a circular dependency where you need high-quality manual annotations to build the tool that reduces annotation burden. Premature algorithmic deployment (before sufficient labeled data exists) risks false-confidence tool promotion; conversely, investing heavily in manual dual-scoring upfront delays Aim 3 algorithm development and stretches the clinical psychologist's and technicians' capacity.
options: Prioritize manual dual-scoring of all flagged events through month 18, deliberately deferring semi-automated tool development until sufficient labeled dataset (n=200–300 adjudicated events) exists; use year two onward to train and validate triage models against this ground truth, accepting slower Aim 3 progress for methodological rigor.

Begin building a lightweight machine-learning triage model in parallel with ongoing manual annotation from month 6 onward, using iterative retraining on accumulating labeled data; accept higher false-positive rates early and refine model specificity as labeled dataset grows, trading methodological perfection for earlier tool availability.

Recruit and fund an independent external team (biomedical signal-processing group at another institution) to develop and validate the event-triage tools using de-identified data provided in batches from the Bonn unit; preserve internal staff focus on participant management and manual annotation, but introduce external coordination overhead and longer development timeline.
levers.review_lever: Building triage tools too early wastes development effort on unreliable models trained on sparse labeled data; delaying tool development until sufficient labeled data exists delays Aim 3 completion; outsourcing tool development offloads burden but introduces coordination complexity and potential publication-priority friction.

levers.name: Publication and Data-Sharing Strategy Timing
levers.consequences: Early publications (targeting 2–3 papers by month 36 per success criteria) based on pilot-cohort methods validation and preliminary longitudinal patterns establish credibility and support Phase 2 funding pitches, but committing to fast-turnaround publication schedules may force compromises on analysis depth or statistical power. Conversely, deferring publication until a mature dataset with 60+ participants is complete (likely beyond 36 months) guarantees robust phenotyping conclusions but delays grant-application windows and risks competitors publishing similar findings or preempting key scientific positions.
options: Commit to publishing a methods-validation paper by month 15 (covering facility safety, capture rate, annotation reliability) and a preliminary longitudinal phenotyping preprint by month 24, accepting data-cutoff constraints and smaller sample sizes (n=20–30) to maintain publication momentum and early Phase 2 funding visibility.

Delay all major publications until month 28–30, when 50+ participants have been enrolled and a mature event dataset with robust inter-rater agreement exists; publish a single comprehensive methods-and-phenotyping manuscript, trading early visibility for scientific comprehensiveness and statistical power.

Pursue a dual-track strategy: submit a rapid methods validation paper by month 18 (limited to facility operations, event-capture rates, and sensor-data quality), followed by later longitudinal phenotyping and Aim 3 algorithm papers as data mature, accepting editorial fragmentation but maintaining publication cadence.
levers.review_lever: Early publication deadlines force premature analysis cutoffs and reduce sample size; delayed publication maximizes statistical power but misses funding windows and risks being preempted by competitors; dual-track approach preserves momentum but spreads findings across multiple venues and complicates funding narrative cohesion.

levers.name: Recruitment Criteria Flexibility and Inclusion Boundaries
levers.consequences: Strict inclusion criteria (confirmed NREM parasomnia via specialist interview and collateral history, 2+ episodes per month) ensure homogeneous, high-yield cohort but narrow recruitment pool, extending enrollment timelines and risking enrollment shortfall (fewer than 25 participants by month 18, triggering external review). Looser criteria (e.g., accepting historical diagnoses without pre-admission polysomnography, reducing episode-frequency thresholds) widen the recruitment pool but introduce phenotypic heterogeneity, increase false-positive admissions, and degrade data quality if borderline cases (suspected-but-unconfirmed sleep-related dissociative episodes) are included.
options: Maintain current criteria strictly (specialist confirmation, 2+ episodes/month, pre-admission screening PSG or prior clinical documentation), accepting slower enrollment; if the 25-participant month-18 threshold is missed, pause enrollment to conduct a protocol amendment that relaxes frequency thresholds (to 1+ episode per month) with ethics approval, creating a recruitment "reset" at month 19.

Prospectively broaden criteria at study launch to include participants with suspected NREM parasomnias based on clinical interview and collateral history alone (waiving requirement for prior/screening PSG), accepting higher screening heterogeneity in exchange for faster recruitment and earlier operational validation.

Establish a two-tier enrollment scheme: Tier 1 (confirmed NREM parasomnia per original strict criteria, target 40 participants) provides the primary Aim 2 phenotyping cohort; Tier 2 (suspected or atypical parasomnias, target 15 participants) enrolls separately with identical monitoring but distinct subgroup analysis, preserving high-yield primary cohort while expanding recruitment reach.
levers.review_lever: Strict criteria ensure phenotypic homogeneity but risk missing enrollment targets and triggering external review; relaxed criteria accelerate recruitment but introduce diagnostic noise and unproductive admissions; a two-tier scheme allows flexibility but complicates analysis stratification and publication narrative.

levers.name: Pharmaceutical Partnership Terms and Intellectual Property Constraints
levers.consequences: A pharma partnership could provide €300K–500K upside funding to offset expansion costs and strengthen year-two operations, but formal partnerships typically introduce publication delays, IP sharing expectations, and scope creep (e.g., requests to add pharma-specific drug-response monitoring arms). The current plan restricts the partner to a 30-day pre-publication comment window, minimizing constraints, but enforcing this boundary during a funded partnership requires explicit contractual language and may be perceived as ungracious by the partner, risking relationship strain or fund withdrawal.
options: Pursue partnership funding early (target negotiations by month 3) with a pre-negotiated contract explicitly separating "core unit research" (NREM parasomnia characterization, event-triage tools, full publication autonomy) from any optional "pharma-specific modules" (separate protocol, separate participant cohort, separate funding line), preserving academic independence while securing upside capital.

Defer pharma partnership discussions until month 18, after Aim 1 facility validation is complete and enrollment trajectory is proven; pursue partnership as a conditional year-2/3 enhancement only if DFG and internal funding shortfalls emerge, avoiding early complexity but risking partnership delays when capital is most needed.

Reject pharmaceutical partnership in principle and rely exclusively on DFG and University of Bonn internal funding; eliminate negotiation complexity and IP friction, but accept tighter budgets and reduced expansion flexibility, with potential staff retention risk if year-two operations tighten significantly.
levers.review_lever: Early pharma partnerships secure upside funding but introduce contractual complexity and potential publication friction; deferred partnerships preserve autonomy but risk capital delays; rejecting pharma funding simplifies governance but constrains operational flexibility and may threaten staff retention if other funding pipelines underperform.

responses.strategic_rationale: This parasomnia research unit's core tension lies between maximizing naturalistic behavior capture (requiring a domestic setting with minimal patient burden) and ensuring rigorous scientific control (demanding comprehensive physiological instrumentation and clinical-grade data curation). The unit must also balance rapid event yield against extended participant stays, participant safety against operational feasibility, and German regulatory compliance against international research collaboration. The levers below address recruitment sustainability, sensor strategy evolution, staffing resilience, regulatory burden, facility optimization, publication timing, and external validation—each navigating the boundary between methodological rigor and operational sustainability.

levers.name: Recruitment Source Diversification and Recruitment-Criteria Stability
levers.consequences: Expanding beyond the University Hospital Bonn sleep clinic and DGSM network to patient advocacy groups, online forums, and international tertiary centers increases absolute referral volume and event yield, but introduces recruitment variability and potential protocol-deviancy challenges if inclusion criteria are not consistently applied across geographically dispersed sources. Reliance on a single clinic pathway offers stability but risks enrollment stalling if that referral source is disrupted by staff turnover or competing studies.
options: Establish a formal multi-site referral network across five German regional sleep centers with standardized pre-screening procedures and quarterly synchronization meetings to harmonize inclusion adjudication.
Maintain recruitment exclusively through University Hospital Bonn and DGSM direct referrals while developing a 6-month lead list of referred patients to buffer against seasonal referral fluctuations.

Create a dedicated patient registry and telephone pre-screening pathway open to self-referrals from parasomnia support communities across German-speaking Europe, with telephone eligibility confirmation by a trained research assistant before formal PI adjudication.
levers.review_lever: Multi-site recruitment accelerates enrollment but demands federated quality control; single-source recruitment is slower but eliminates cross-site adjudication drift, risking a shortfall if that source dries up unexpectedly.

levers.name: Dry-Electrode Headband Validation and Rollout Cadence
levers.consequences: Dry-electrode EEG headbands reduce participant setup burden and improve tolerability during extended stays, but their signal fidelity for detecting parasomnia-associated arousals and motor phenomena remains unproven in this population and under the current protocol design. Early rollout accelerates the low-burden monitoring pathway but risks accumulating unreliable baseline EEG across pilot participants; delayed validation prolongs reliance on standard PSG montages on enhanced nights, increasing cost-per-participant and pushing full-study data collection further into year two.
options: Deploy dry-electrode headbands to all participants beginning month 3 after a 10-participant pilot comparison study validates signal quality against simultaneous standard scalp EEG, accepting a 2-month delay in full pilot enrollment to secure technical confidence.

Restrict dry-electrode headbands to non-critical monitoring nights and research cohort exploratory phases, reserving standard scalp EEG for all three scheduled enhanced nights per participant throughout the 3-year period.

Conduct in-parallel signal quality benchmarking on months 3–6 participants using simultaneous dry-electrode and standard EEG without disrupting enrollment, then make a binary rollout decision by month 7 based on comparative sensitivity and artifact burden data.
levers.review_lever: Early deployment without full validation risks low-fidelity baseline EEG contaminating phenotyping analyses; delayed deployment preserves data quality but locks the study into costlier PSG montages, reducing efficiency and delaying publication timelines.

levers.name: Night Technician Skill and Annotation-Burden Triage
levers.consequences: As event volume accumulates, manual real-time annotation and dual-scoring become the bottleneck in the critical path, directly constraining either throughput or annotation quality. Investing in technician training and event-flagging decision support reduces review time but requires months of skill development; outsourcing annotation to independent scorers distributes workload but adds per-event cost and communication overhead.
options: Establish a 6-week on-site technician training program at month 2 covering AASM parasomnia morphology recognition, event flagging decision trees, and quality-control protocols, with monthly competency reassessment and cross-validation with the PI to standardize annotation decisions.

Hire two full-time independent sleep-scored technicians by month 4 working asynchronously to score nightly event flags submitted by shift technicians, physically segregating real-time flagging from later-stage formal scoring to reduce cognitive conflict and improve dual-rater agreement.

Implement a lightweight event-triage pre-filtering tool beginning month 5 that ranks sensor-detected candidate events by parasomnia probability before technician assignment, allowing technicians to focus dual-scoring effort on high-confidence candidates and defer low-confidence events to a secondary-review backlog.
levers.review_lever: Technician training is cost-efficient but demands sustained mentorship and risks inconsistency across shifts; independent scoring adds cost per-event; event-triage filtering requires algorithmic development upfront but offers scalability as participant volume grows.

levers.name: Extended-Stay Protocol Flexibility and Participant Retention Risk
levers.consequences: Offering stays of up to 10 weeks (with extensions beyond the initial 2–8 week period for zero-event participants) increases the probability of capturing infrequent parasomnia events and reduces the failure-trigger risk of unproductive admissions, but extended stays strain participant morale, introduce confounding from habituation and sleep-deprivation effects, and reduce turnover capacity. Shorter fixed stays simplify operations but risk higher unproductive-admission rates and potential protocol review by month 18.
options: Adopt a fixed 6-week stay duration for all participants with no extensions, accepting that approximately 15–20% may depart without captured events, and treat unproductive admissions as a recruitment-enrichment signal rather than a protocol failure.

Implement a tiered extension pathway: offer 2-week extensions only to participants meeting predefined engagement and safety criteria (e.g., high adherence, no safety incidents, explicit consent for extended stay), capping total stay at 8 weeks for any participant and conducting weekly morale check-ins by the clinical psychologist.

Allow participant-initiated stay extensions up to 10 weeks on a case-by-case basis negotiated with each participant at week 4, with formal psychological assessment before approval, framing extended stay as a voluntary research partnership rather than a study requirement.
levers.review_lever: Fixed stays optimize operational predictability but risk high unproductive-admission rates and triggering month-18 external review; extensions capture more events but introduce habituation confounding and morale risk, requiring careful psychological monitoring.

levers.name: Neuroimaging Modality Integration and Budget Allocation
levers.consequences: Adding functional MRI, DTI, or structural neuroimaging on baseline and post-stay evaluations would strengthen phenotyping and mechanistic hypotheses but requires coordination with hospital MRI scheduling, adds €200–400 per participant, and introduces anatomical confounders not directly relevant to event capture. Deferring neuroimaging to a phase-two grant proposal preserves budget for core event-capture operations and keeps the current study focused on electrophysiological phenotyping, but limits cross-domain mechanistic insights.
options: Establish a voluntary neuroimaging sub-study co-enrolled with 20 participants across years two and three using existing University Hospital Bonn MRI capacity, with independent funding negotiated with the Department of Neurology, keeping core-unit budget protected for event capture and staffing.

Exclude all neuroimaging from the current protocol and position advanced neuroimaging as an explicit phase-two goal, framing the current unit as a phenotyping-and-methods platform that de-risks later mechanistic studies and strengthens future neuroimaging grant applications.

Implement a single structural MRI scan on a subset of 15 participants (baseline only, no post-stay) using a rapid 5-minute protocol at zero incremental cost by integrating with routine clinical brain MRI scheduling, creating a limited anatomical reference dataset without diverting event-capture resources.
levers.review_lever: Systematic neuroimaging strengthens mechanistic claims but risks draining limited budget and complicating coordination; deferral simplifies the current protocol and concentrates resources on event capture, but limits interim neurobiological insights for publications.

levers.name: Pharmaceutical Partnership Engagement and Confidentiality Walls
levers.consequences: Accepting pharmaceutical industry sponsorship for the event-triage algorithm development (e.g., conditional on demonstrating 85% sensitivity for parasomnia detection) accelerates algorithm refinement and provides contingency revenue, but introduces contractual confidentiality windows, publication-timing constraints, and the risk of algorithm results being withheld if they show efficacy for a competing pharmacotherapy target. Rejecting pharma partnerships preserves full scientific independence and publication timing but reduces contingency revenue and forces algorithm development to be powered only by the €800K year-three conditional budget.
options: Pursue a narrowly scoped pharmaceutical collaboration for event-triage algorithm development only, with a contractual pre-publication window of 15 days (reduced from the default 30 days), a public-domain algorithm release guarantee by month 36, and a firewall prohibiting pharma input on participant selection, clinical outcome definitions, or phenotyping publications.

Decline any pharmaceutical partnership during the current 3-year protocol and reserve pharmaceutical collaboration exclusively for post-study intervention trials in phase two, preserving complete independence and publication autonomy during the foundational methods and phenotyping work.

Accept a pharmaceutical partnership contingent on them funding the independent-scoring technicians (€150K over 3 years) as a neutral infrastructure investment, with explicit contractual separation between pharma-funded personnel and any algorithm or phenotyping intellectual property development.
levers.review_lever: Pharma funding accelerates algorithm development and provides budget insurance, but introduces publication-timing risk and potential conflict if algorithm results compete with pharma's therapeutic targets; full independence is slower but guarantees publication autonomy.

levers.name: Matched Control Enrollment and Protocol Burden
levers.consequences: Recruiting and managing a parallel matched-control cohort (age, sex, sleep duration, occupational factors) sleeping in the same suites under identical monitoring conditions is essential for benchmarking the event-triage tool's false-positive rate and distinguishing parasomnia-specific physiological signatures from normal nocturnal behavior. However, controls must be asymptomatic and deeply screened for occult sleep disorders, adding recruitment complexity, and their overnight stays compete for suite capacity during the pilot phase when occupancy is constrained. Deferring controls to year two simplifies year-one operations but delays the external validation necessary for robust algorithm benchmarking.
options: Recruit matched controls beginning month 6 at a 1:1 ratio with parasomnia participants (targeting 10–15 controls by end of year one), housed during off-peak weeks when parasomnia enrollments are between cohorts, and collected in a dedicated control-annotated dataset to avoid contamination of parasomnia case phenotypes.

Postpone control recruitment until month 18 and enroll matched controls exclusively during year two and three at a 1:2 ratio to parasomnia participants, enabling full suite utilization for active cases in year one while still permitting algorithm benchmarking by mid-study.

Develop a lightweight home-based control actigraphy arm using wrist actigraphy and smartphone sleep logs from community volunteers outside the residential unit, avoiding suite-occupancy competition but sacrificing the video and infrared sensor data necessary for full false-positive benchmarking.
levers.review_lever: Parallel 1:1 controls provide robust algorithm benchmarking but constrain suite capacity during the pilot phase; deferred controls preserve year-one enrollment momentum but delay external-validation data; home-based controls are cost-efficient but lack video/IR data needed for comprehensive false-positive assessment.

levers.consequences: A pharma partnership could provide €300K–500K upside funding to offset expansion costs and strengthen year-two operations, but formal partnerships typically introduce publication delays, IP sharing expectations, and scope creep (e.g., requests to add pharma-specific drug-response monitoring arms). The current plan restricts the partner to a 30-day pre-publication comment window, minimizing constraints, but enforcing this boundary during a funded partnership requires explicit contractual language and may be perceived as ungracious by the partner, risking relationship strain or fund withdrawal.
options: Pursue partnership funding early (target negotiations by month 3) with a pre-negotiated contract explicitly separating "core unit research" (NREM parasomnia characterization, event-triage tools, full publication autonomy) from any optional "pharma-specific modules" (separate protocol, separate participant cohort, separate funding line), preserving academic independence while securing upside capital.

Defer pharma partnership discussions until month 18, after Aim 1 facility validation is complete and enrollment trajectory is proven; pursue partnership as a conditional year-2/3 enhancement only if DFG and internal funding shortfalls emerge, avoiding early complexity but risking partnership delays when capital is most needed.

Reject pharmaceutical partnership in principle and rely exclusively on DFG and University of Bonn internal funding; eliminate negotiation complexity and IP friction, but accept tighter budgets and reduced expansion flexibility, with potential staff retention risk if year-two operations tighten significantly.
levers.review: Early pharma partnerships secure upside funding but introduce contractual complexity and potential publication friction; deferred partnerships preserve autonomy but risk capital delays; rejecting pharma funding simplifies governance but constrains operational flexibility and may threaten staff retention if other funding pipelines underperform.

levers.name: Recruitment Source Diversification and Recruitment-Criteria Stability
levers.consequences: Expanding beyond the University Hospital Bonn sleep clinic and DGSM network to patient advocacy groups, online forums, and international tertiary centers increases absolute referral volume and event yield, but introduces recruitment variability and potential protocol-deviancy challenges if inclusion criteria are not consistently applied across geographically dispersed sources. Reliance on a single clinic pathway offers stability but risks enrollment stalling if that referral source is disrupted by staff turnover or competing studies.
options: Establish a formal multi-site referral network across five German regional sleep centers with standardized pre-screening procedures and quarterly synchronization meetings to harmonize inclusion adjudication.
Maintain recruitment exclusively through University Hospital Bonn and DGSM direct referrals while developing a 6-month lead list of referred patients to buffer against seasonal referral fluctuations.

Create a dedicated patient registry and telephone pre-screening pathway open to self-referrals from parasomnia support communities across German-speaking Europe, with telephone eligibility confirmation by a trained research assistant before formal PI adjudication.
levers.review: Multi-site recruitment accelerates enrollment but demands federated quality control; single-source recruitment is slower but eliminates cross-site adjudication drift, risking a shortfall if that source dries up unexpectedly.

levers.name: Dry-Electrode Headband Validation and Rollout Cadence
levers.consequences: Dry-electrode EEG headbands reduce participant setup burden and improve tolerability during extended stays, but their signal fidelity for detecting parasomnia-associated arousals and motor phenomena remains unproven in this population and under the current protocol design. Early rollout accelerates the low-burden monitoring pathway but risks accumulating unreliable baseline EEG across pilot participants; delayed validation prolongs reliance on standard PSG montages on enhanced nights, increasing cost-per-participant and pushing full-study data collection further into year two.
options: Deploy dry-electrode headbands to all participants beginning month 3 after a 10-participant pilot comparison study validates signal quality against simultaneous standard scalp EEG, accepting a 2-month delay in full pilot enrollment to secure technical confidence.

Restrict dry-electrode headbands to non-critical monitoring nights and research cohort exploratory phases, reserving standard scalp EEG for all three scheduled enhanced nights per participant throughout the 3-year period.

Conduct in-parallel signal quality benchmarking on months 3–6 participants using simultaneous dry-electrode and standard EEG without disrupting enrollment, then make a binary rollout decision by month 7 based on comparative sensitivity and artifact burden data.
levers.review: Early deployment without full validation risks low-fidelity baseline EEG contaminating phenotyping analyses; delayed deployment preserves data quality but locks the study into costlier PSG montages, reducing efficiency and delaying publication timelines.

levers.name: Night Technician Skill and Annotation-Burden Triage
levers.consequences: As event volume accumulates, manual real-time annotation and dual-scoring become the bottleneck in the critical path, directly constraining either throughput or annotation quality. Investing in technician training and event-flagging decision support reduces review time but requires months of skill development; outsourcing annotation to independent scorers distributes workload but adds per-event cost and communication overhead.
options: Establish a 6-week on-site technician training program at month 2 covering AASM parasomnia morphology recognition, event flagging decision trees, and quality-control protocols, with monthly competency reassessment and cross-validation with the PI to standardize annotation decisions.

Hire two full-time independent sleep-scored technicians by month 4 working asynchronously to score nightly event flags submitted by shift technicians, physically segregating real-time flagging from later-stage formal scoring to reduce cognitive conflict and improve dual-rater agreement.

Implement a lightweight event-triage pre-filtering tool beginning month 5 that ranks sensor-detected candidate events by parasomnia probability before technician assignment, allowing technicians to focus dual-scoring effort on high-confidence candidates and defer low-confidence events to a secondary-review backlog.
levers.review: Technician training is cost-efficient but demands sustained mentorship and risks inconsistency across shifts; independent scoring adds cost per-event; event-triage filtering requires algorithmic development upfront but offers scalability as participant volume grows.

levers.name: Extended-Stay Protocol Flexibility and Participant Retention Risk
levers.consequences: Offering stays of up to 10 weeks (with extensions beyond the initial 2–8 week period for zero-event participants) increases the probability of capturing infrequent parasomnia events and reduces the failure-trigger risk of unproductive admissions, but extended stays strain participant morale, introduce confounding from habituation and sleep-deprivation effects, and reduce turnover capacity. Shorter fixed stays simplify operations but risk higher unproductive-admission rates and potential protocol review by month 18.
options: Adopt a fixed 6-week stay duration for all participants with no extensions, accepting that approximately 15–20% may depart without captured events, and treat unproductive admissions as a recruitment-enrichment signal rather than a protocol failure.

Implement a tiered extension pathway: offer 2-week extensions only to participants meeting predefined engagement and safety criteria (e.g., high adherence, no safety incidents, explicit consent for extended stay), capping total stay at 8 weeks for any participant and conducting weekly morale check-ins by the clinical psychologist.

Allow participant-initiated stay extensions up to 10 weeks on a case-by-case basis negotiated with each participant at week 4, with formal psychological assessment before approval, framing extended stay as a voluntary research partnership rather than a study requirement.
levers.review: Fixed stays optimize operational predictability but risk high unproductive-admission rates and triggering month-18 external review; extensions capture more events but introduce habituation confounding and morale risk, requiring careful psychological monitoring.

levers.name: Neuroimaging Modality Integration and Budget Allocation
levers.consequences: Adding functional MRI, DTI, or structural neuroimaging on baseline and post-stay evaluations would strengthen phenotyping and mechanistic hypotheses but requires coordination with hospital MRI scheduling, adds €200–400 per participant, and introduces anatomical confounders not directly relevant to event capture. Deferring neuroimaging to a phase-two grant proposal preserves budget for core event-capture operations and keeps the current study focused on electrophysiological phenotyping, but limits cross-domain mechanistic insights.
options: Establish a voluntary neuroimaging sub-study co-enrolled with 20 participants across years two and three using existing University Hospital Bonn MRI capacity, with independent funding negotiated with the Department of Neurology, keeping core-unit budget protected for event capture and staffing.

Exclude all neuroimaging from the current protocol and position advanced neuroimaging as an explicit phase-two goal, framing the current unit as a phenotyping-and-methods platform that de-risks later mechanistic studies and strengthens future neuroimaging grant applications.

Implement a single structural MRI scan on a subset of 15 participants (baseline only, no post-stay) using a rapid 5-minute protocol at zero incremental cost by integrating with routine clinical brain MRI scheduling, creating a limited anatomical reference dataset without diverting event-capture resources.
levers.review: Systematic neuroimaging strengthens mechanistic claims but risks draining limited budget and complicating coordination; deferral simplifies the current protocol and concentrates resources on event capture, but limits interim neurobiological insights for publications.

levers.name: Pharmaceutical Partnership Engagement and Confidentiality Walls
levers.consequences: Accepting pharmaceutical industry sponsorship for the event-triage algorithm development (e.g., conditional on demonstrating 85% sensitivity for parasomnia detection) accelerates algorithm refinement and provides contingency revenue, but introduces contractual confidentiality windows, publication-timing constraints, and the risk of algorithm results being withheld if they show efficacy for a competing pharmacotherapy target. Rejecting pharma partnerships preserves full scientific independence and publication timing but reduces contingency revenue and forces algorithm development to be powered only by the €800K year-three conditional budget.
options: Pursue a narrowly scoped pharmaceutical collaboration for event-triage algorithm development only, with a contractual pre-publication window of 15 days (reduced from the default 30 days), a public-domain algorithm release guarantee by month 36, and a firewall prohibiting pharma input on participant selection, clinical outcome definitions, or phenotyping publications.

Decline any pharmaceutical partnership during the current 3-year protocol and reserve pharmaceutical collaboration exclusively for post-study intervention trials in phase two, preserving complete independence and publication autonomy during the foundational methods and phenotyping work.

Accept a pharmaceutical partnership contingent on them funding the independent-scoring technicians (€150K over 3 years) as a neutral infrastructure investment, with explicit contractual separation between pharma-funded personnel and any algorithm or phenotyping intellectual property development.
levers.review: Pharma funding accelerates algorithm development and provides budget insurance, but introduces publication-timing risk and potential conflict if algorithm results compete with pharma's therapeutic targets; full independence is slower but guarantees publication autonomy.

levers.name: Matched Control Enrollment and Protocol Burden
levers.consequences: Recruiting and managing a parallel matched-control cohort (age, sex, sleep duration, occupational factors) sleeping in the same suites under identical monitoring conditions is essential for benchmarking the event-triage tool's false-positive rate and distinguishing parasomnia-specific physiological signatures from normal nocturnal behavior. However, controls must be asymptomatic and deeply screened for occult sleep disorders, adding recruitment complexity, and their overnight stays compete for suite capacity during the pilot phase when occupancy is constrained. Deferring controls to year two simplifies year-one operations but delays the external validation necessary for robust algorithm benchmarking.
options: Recruit matched controls beginning month 6 at a 1:1 ratio with parasomnia participants (targeting 10–15 controls by end of year one), housed during off-peak weeks when parasomnia enrollments are between cohorts, and collected in a dedicated control-annotated dataset to avoid contamination of parasomnia case phenotypes.

Postpone control recruitment until month 18 and enroll matched controls exclusively during year two and three at a 1:2 ratio to parasomnia participants, enabling full suite utilization for active cases in year one while still permitting algorithm benchmarking by mid-study.

Develop a lightweight home-based control actigraphy arm using wrist actigraphy and smartphone sleep logs from community volunteers outside the residential unit, avoiding suite-occupancy competition but sacrificing the video and infrared sensor data necessary for full false-positive benchmarking.
levers.review: Parallel 1:1 controls provide robust algorithm benchmarking but constrain suite capacity during the pilot phase; deferred controls preserve year-one enrollment momentum but delay external-validation data; home-based controls are cost-efficient but lack video/IR data needed for comprehensive false-positive assessment.

Plan:
Establish a 3-year residential longitudinal research unit in Bonn, Germany, for the study of adult NREM parasomnias — sleepwalking, confusional arousals, and sleep terrors — with a secondary exploratory arm for REM sleep behavior disorder under a separate protocol with dedicated neurologic screening, reflecting RBD's distinct clinical trajectory per current AASM guidance. The facility is affiliated with University Hospital Bonn's Department of Epileptology, leveraging its existing long-term video-EEG monitoring culture, and addresses a specific methodological gap: traditional single-night polysomnography rarely captures infrequent parasomnia events, while outpatient actigraphy lacks physiological resolution. The unit houses 8 active sleep suites at launch in a converted residential property in a quiet Bonn neighborhood, renovated for safety (padded corridor edges, restricted-opening windows, silent exterior door alarms, fire safety, acoustic treatment, network cabling, accessibility modifications) while preserving a domestic feel — if the environment is too clinical, naturalistic behavior is suppressed. Physical capacity exists for 12 suites, but expansion is deferred until the pilot proves acceptable data quality, manageable false alarm rates, safe staffing ratios, and usable annotation throughput. Sensing uses a tiered acquisition model: nightly low-burden monitoring via dry-electrode EEG headbands, contact-free mattress sensors, unobtrusively mounted infrared cameras, ambient microphones, and environmental sensors; scheduled enhanced nights with fuller PSG montage including standard scalp EEG, EOG, chin EMG, and leg EMG on the first night, one mid-stay night, and the final night per participant; and escalation nights deploying full PSG after technician-flagged events to capture recurrence at clinical-grade resolution. All streams are time-synchronized and stored in EEG-BIDS-compatible format on a local NAS with nightly encrypted backup to university storage, annotated in real time by the night technician and later scored by two independent raters using AASM criteria with inter-rater reliability reported. Public data sharing is limited to de-identified physiological and sensor data under data use agreements — bedroom video carries severe privacy constraints and is not deposited in public repositories. The scientific program has three explicit aims: Aim 1, establish and operationally validate the residential capture model as safe, ethics-approved, and sustainable; Aim 2, characterize within-person and between-person parasomnia patterns longitudinally, including episode frequency, morphology, triggers, and temporal clustering; Aim 3, develop and benchmark semi-automated event-triage tools that rank probable parasomnia episodes and reduce manual review burden, evaluated against dual human scorer agreement rather than promising autonomous diagnosis.

Participant recruitment targets adults aged 18–65 with NREM parasomnia confirmed through a structured pre-admission pathway: specialist clinical interview, collateral history from bed partner or household member where available, prior or screening polysomnography, and a structured exclusion checklist adjudicated by the PI. Explicit exclusions are nocturnal epilepsy or suspected epilepsy mimics, untreated obstructive sleep apnea, active major substance use disorder, severe psychiatric instability, and wandering or injury risk beyond facility capability. Recruitment channels are the University Hospital Bonn sleep clinic, regional neurologist referrals, and the Deutsche Gesellschaft für Schlafforschung und Schlafmedizin network, with per-night compensation of €80 plus meals. A matched control group provides baseline nocturnal movement, arousal patterns, and false-positive sensor activity under identical residential monitoring conditions, enabling benchmarking of the event-triage tools against normal nocturnal behavior. Event-yield planning assumes that based on the inclusion criterion of at least 2 self-reported episodes per month, approximately 70–80% of admitted participants will produce at least one captured and adjudicated event during a 2–8 week stay; stays may be extended up to 2 additional weeks for participants with zero captured events after the initial period, capped at 10 weeks total, with a protocol ceiling of 20% unproductive admissions before triggering a recruitment-criteria review. The core team is 9 people: a PI who is a board-certified sleep medicine physician, 2 postdoctoral researchers in sleep neurophysiology and computational neuroscience respectively, 3 research technicians rotating night shifts to ensure safe coverage of 8 active suites with adequate margin for event response and annotation, a clinical psychologist specializing in sleep disorders, a data engineer managing the sensor pipeline, and a study coordinator handling recruitment, consent, scheduling, and ethics compliance.

Budget is €3.8 million over 3 years, gated: €1.8M year one covering property lease and renovation at approximately €750K, equipment at approximately €450K, staff hiring accounting for German social insurance contributions and actual overnight coverage, ethics approval, and a pilot cohort of 15–20 participants; €1.2M year two covering full operations with 30–35 participants, the enhanced-night PSG program, first publications, and event-triage algorithm development; €800K year three conditional on demonstrable progress by month 24. Personnel costs are approximately €2M over three years and remaining funds cover participant compensation, independent scoring time, data storage and retention, regulatory and legal work, and contingency. Funding sources are DFG research grant and University of Bonn internal research funding as the primary pillars, with a pharmaceutical industry partnership as optional upside rather than a feasibility requirement — if secured, the academic team retains full publication rights with the pharma partner receiving a 30-day pre-publication comment window only. Success criteria at 36 months: safe residential monitoring operations sustained for at least 24 months, enrollment of 50–70 NREM parasomnia participants plus matched controls, capture of a prespecified minimum number of independently adjudicated parasomnia events sufficient for Aim 2 phenotyping analysis, 2–3 peer-reviewed publications in sleep medicine journals covering methods validation and longitudinal characterization, a benchmarked semi-automated event-triage model with reported sensitivity, specificity, and agreement against dual human scoring, de-identified physiological dataset deposited in a recognized repository, and a submitted phase-two grant proposal for expansion and intervention studies. Failure triggers: if by month 18 the facility has enrolled fewer than 25 participants or captured fewer than 40 adjudicated events, the program undergoes external review. Governance is a 3-member external scientific advisory board reviewing progress every 6 months, with the PI holding operational authority and budget reallocations above €50K requiring board approval. Banned words: AI, blockchain, app, VR, AR, gamification, wearable startup, consumer product, DAO, NFT, metaverse, smart home, autonomous diagnosis, digital therapeutic, SaaS, marketplace, validated (in the context of claiming a mature deployable system). Pick a realistic scenario — this is an early-stage clinical research facility producing methods validation and phenotyping work, not a finished diagnostic platform.
